questions.q: Why does LTV Global organize metadata into unlocked packages, one per business unit?
options: So each BU can deploy and version its own changes independently, without bundling in another BU's in-progress work, while still deploying into the single shared org
Because unlocked packages are required for any org with more than 1,000 users
Because each business unit needs its own completely separate Salesforce org
Because packages eliminate the need for Apex tests
questions.explain: Per-BU packaging lets each business unit ship changes to its own package independently, with its own version history, while shared metadata lives in a common package every BU package depends on.

questions.q: What happens before any change is eligible to reach production, per this lesson's CI pipeline?
options: Only a manual peer review is required; automated testing is optional
Automated Apex tests run in a clean environment and must pass before the change is eligible for release — this is a gate, not a courtesy step
The change goes directly from a developer's scratch org to production
Only changes touching the integration hub require any testing at all
questions.explain: The lesson states explicitly that automated Apex tests are a gate: no change reaches production without passing them first, regardless of which BU package it belongs to.

questions.q: How does LTV Global's release cadence relate to Salesforce's own seasonal release calendar?
options: LTV Global ignores Salesforce's release calendar entirely
LTV Global tests each BU package against a preview of the upcoming Salesforce release, while running its own more frequent release trains within that platform-level cadence
LTV Global only releases changes three times per year, exactly matching Salesforce's cycle
Salesforce's release calendar has no effect on any Salesforce customer's own release cadence
questions.explain: LTV Global aligns to Salesforce's seasonal calendar for platform-level compatibility testing, but runs its own more frequent internal release trains for BU feature work, since waiting for Salesforce's cycle would badly mismatch active BU teams' pace.

questions.q: Why does LTV Global's Change Advisory Board (CAB) exist specifically, per this lesson?
options: Because every Salesforce org is legally required to have a CAB
Because the single global org (Lesson 7) means one BU's release touching shared metadata or the integration hub can affect every other BU
Because the CAB replaces the need for automated Apex tests
Because CABs are required only for changes to Experience Cloud sites
questions.explain: The CAB exists as a direct consequence of the single-org decision: shared-platform risk means releases touching shared metadata or the integration hub need cross-functional review before reaching production.

questions.q: Per this lesson, which kinds of changes do NOT require full CAB review?
options: Any change at all, since the CAB reviews every single release
Changes that touch only one BU's own package with no shared dependency
Changes to the integration hub specifically
Changes to shared, cross-BU metadata like the core Equipment Asset object
questions.explain: BU-specific changes with no shared dependency can move faster without full CAB review, which keeps the CAB from becoming a bottleneck on every single change while still gating genuinely cross-cutting risk.
